standard.title: Collaborate and manage projects
standard.description: Select and use appropriate digital tools effectively to share content online, plan tasks and collaborate on projects, demonstrating agreed behaviours
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can use the core features of common digital tools to share content, plan tasks and collaborate, following agreed rules (AC9TDI4P07). They have used shared tools with provided rules. They have not yet selected tools themselves or taken ownership of defining and moderating collaborative behaviours.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students select appropriate tools for sharing content and project collaboration, manage files and project tasks, and demonstrate agreed online behaviours including cultural protocols and respect for others' work.

nodes.label: Organising and managing files for shared access
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can organise and store shared files in a way that allows collaborators to locate and use them easily
nodes.minimum_width: Organise a set of project files using folders and consistent naming so that a collaborator can locate a specific file
nodes.typical_width: Create a folder structure for a project with logical hierarchy (e.g. main topic → sub-sections) and consistent file naming; explain the naming and organisation decisions in terms of how collaborators will access the files
wider: Design a folder structure for a school garden project with multiple teams — ensuring each team can find shared resources without access conflicts or confusion about which version is current
Compare two approaches to file organisation (flat folder with long filenames vs deep hierarchy with short names) and explain which is more effective for a given team size and project scope

response_modes.reason: File organisation is a habit-formation task — students understand the principle quickly but apply it inconsistently without deliberate practice. Consistency across multiple projects is more important than correctness on a single task.

success_criteria: Creates at least one folder with a logical sub-folder structure
Files are named consistently and can be located by purpose

nodes.label: Demonstrating agreed online behaviours
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can define and follow agreed online community standards when collaborating in a digital environment
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two agreed behaviours for online collaboration (e.g. not deleting others' work, using appropriate language) and explain why each matters
nodes.typical_width: Define collective standards for an online collaboration, including appropriate language, not modifying others' work without permission, respecting intellectual property, and acknowledging sources; apply these consistently in a collaborative project
wider: Moderate language and behaviour in an online class forum — explaining the decisions made and connecting them to the agreed community standards
Apply cultural protocols when sharing images or information about First Nations Australians' cultural artefacts — identifying what permissions and attributions are required and why they matter

response_modes.reason: Agreed behaviours can feel abstract until students encounter a real breach. Contexts where the consequence of poor behaviour is visible — deleted work, inappropriate content in a shared document, cultural artefacts used without attribution — make the agreed standards meaningful rather than procedural.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations cultural protocols direction (from the elaboration) is rich — it raises substantive questions about permission, attribution and cultural ownership that go beyond general 'be nice online' frameworks, making agreed behaviours principled rather than just procedural.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two agreed online behaviours with reasons
Demonstrates the behaviours in a collaborative task without being reminded

nodes.label: Sharing content with stakeholders using appropriate tools
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select and use an appropriate communication tool to share content with a specific stakeholder audience
nodes.minimum_width: Share a piece of project work with an audience beyond the class using a digital tool; explain why the tool chosen was appropriate for that audience
nodes.typical_width: Use a range of communication tools to share project content with different stakeholders (e.g. presenting to a parents and citizens meeting via online forum, reporting to a local council via email or document sharing); match the tool and format to the audience and purpose
wider: Present content for a school celebration to parents/guardians and school leadership via an online forum — adapting the format and tools to suit an audience that includes both technical and non-technical participants
Report findings about a local government issue (e.g. best location for a skate park) as a small group presentation — choosing tools that support group contribution and audience access

response_modes.reason: Students who have only shared work with peers struggle to adapt to a wider stakeholder audience. Presenting to a parents and citizens meeting or school leadership requires different tool choices, format decisions, and tone than classroom sharing — multiple audience contexts build this adaptability.

success_criteria: Selects a tool appropriate for the specified audience and purpose
Shares content in a format the audience can access and engage with
